summary: This note surveys creation myths from cultures across Africa, Asia, Australia, Scandinavia, North America, Mesoamerica and Polynesia, each tied to a named narrator or scholar and a date in late 2023. It describes how each tradition explains the world's origin, from cosmic eggs and primordial waters to giants' bodies and maize. It concludes that the myths share themes of chaos and order, elemental interplay, sacrifice and fertility, and remain living philosophies.
one_line: A survey of creation myths from African, Asian, Aboriginal, Norse, Navajo, Maya and Polynesian traditions and the themes they share.
key_facts: The Dogon people of Mali believe the world was born from a cosmic egg created by the supreme deity Amma, which burst open to release twins symbolizing the duality of existence; anthropologist Emmanuelle Kady chronicled this on September 25, 2023.

In the Kuba Kingdom (Democratic Republic of Congo) tale, Mbombo ruled a primordial world of water and darkness and vomited the sun, moon, stars, and eventually flora and fauna; Prof. Henry Owusu detailed it on October 3, 2023.
In the Ifugao tale of the Philippines, told by elder Domingo Lam-co on October 12, 2023, the sky met the sea and their union gave birth to the first humans, Wigan and Bugan.
In the Chinese Pangu myth, Pangu emerged from an egg-shaped cosmos and separated yin and yang, earth and heavens, by growing tall over 18,000 years; his body became mountains, rivers, wind, and rain.
Aboriginal elder William Cooper explained on November 4, 2023 that ancestral spirits shaped the world during Dreamtime, creating landscapes, laws, and totems.

In the Norse myth, as told by historian Ragnhild Svensson on November 17, 2023, the void Ginnungagap lay between Muspell (fire) and Niflheim (ice); their meeting produced the frost giant Ymir and the cosmic cow Audhumla.
In the Norse myth, Odin and his brothers slew Ymir and formed the world from his body parts.

Raquel Two-Bears recited a Navajo story on November 25, 2023 in which first beings passed through three dark worlds to reach the fourth, glittering world, where Spider Woman taught them to weave reality from sunlight, lightning, and clouds.
The Quiché Maya of Guatemala myth, described by archaeologist Carlos Mendez on December 5, 2023, says the gods tried to make a worshipping being from mud and wood before succeeding with maize.

Dr. Kiana I'o recounted on December 16, 2023 the Hawaiian belief that the world began in darkness called Po, from which sky father Wakea and earth mother Papa emerged and gave rise to the islands and inhabitants.

The note identifies shared themes across the myths: chaos and order, the interplay of elements, anthropomorphic nature, sacrifice, fertility, divine intervention, and the bond between humans and nature.
The note's exploration is framed as of September 15, 2023 and emphasizes underrepresented creation myths.
